implementation_notes: System.Threading.Channels (in the shared framework since .NET Core 3.0) supplies the mailbox: Channel.CreateBounded with SingleReader = true and an explicit FullMode is the actor's queue, while a class owns the state and one async loop awaits reader.ReadAllAsync() and handles each message to completion. Bounded channels give backpressure (writers await space), bounded overflow modes give drop policies, and ChannelClosedException/Complete mark shutdown. The classic actor object is replaced by the class + channel + loop trio; keep the full framework only when you need addressing, supervision, placement and persistence - which is what Orleans provides.
pitfalls: The channel's FullMode decides overload behavior (Wait, DropNewest, DropOldest, DropWrite); an unbounded channel instead turns overload into OutOfMemoryException.
Forgetting SingleReader = true or starting a second consumer loop breaks the one-message-at-a-time guarantee and reintroduces races on the actor state.
An exception escaping the consumer loop stops the actor silently unless failure handling (restart, dead letter, completion) is explicit.

variants.name: Orleans grain (virtual actor across silos)
variants.implementation_notes: Orleans is a distributed actor framework in which a grain is a virtual actor: identity is a stable user-defined key (IGrainWithGuidKey and friends), the runtime activates the grain on demand on some silo, and messages are asynchronous interface calls queued in the grain's mailbox and processed one at a time, so grain state needs no locks. The managed lifecycle activates, places, deactivates and re-activates grains transparently, and state persists through grain storage. Choose Orleans when actors must survive placement, activation and server failures across a cluster; for a single process the channel variant is far lighter (the Orleans 7/8/9/10 lines target .NET 7+ / .NET 8+ and need a cluster and storage providers).
pitfalls: Grain calls are non-reentrant by default, but [Reentrant], [AlwaysInterleave] or [MayInterleave] enables interleaving at await points; then a read-modify-write sequence spanning an await is not atomic even though each turn is single-threaded.
An idle grain is deactivated and its in-memory state discarded unless it was written to storage; do not treat activation state as durable.
Blocking a grain call (sync-over-async or long CPU work) stalls that grain's mailbox and every caller behind it.
